title: Financial services competence requirements by country: Australia, the EU and Portugal, the US, Japan and the UAE compared
description: How qualification, exam, CPD and continuing education rules for advisers, sales staff and senior managers compare across five financial markets in 2026.
shortAnswer: All five markets require financial services staff who advise or sell to be demonstrably competent, through different models. Australia requires degrees, a professional year and 40 yearly CPD hours for personal advisers. The EU sets qualification and experience standards (MiFID II) and 15 yearly CPD hours for insurance distribution. The United States relies on exams plus annual continuing education. Japan registers exam qualified sales staff with five yearly renewal training. UAE free zones set yearly CPD for key officers.
keyTakeaways: Australia has the most demanding entry standard for personal advisers: an approved degree, a professional year of at least 100 hours of structured training and 1,500 hours of work, then at least 40 CPD hours a year.

Explicit yearly CPD hours appear in Australia (40 for relevant providers), the EU Insurance Distribution Directive (at least 15) and the DFSA (15 for the SEO, Compliance Officer and MLRO); FINRA's Regulatory Element is annual but set by content, not hours.

MiFID II takes a qualification plus experience approach: at least six months of appropriate experience, supervision for at most four years until then, and an annual review of each person's development needs.

Japan works through registration: securities sales representatives must pass the JSDA exam and complete renewal training every five years, and life insurance solicitors complete annual continuing education.
Groups should standardize the competence framework and record model, and localize qualifications, exams, hours and registration, which cannot transfer between markets.

sections.heading: How do financial services competence rules compare by market?

blocks.text: Every market regulates competence for people who advise or sell, but the mechanism differs: Australia and the EU set qualification standards, the United States and Japan rely on exams and registration, and the UAE free zones put competence duties on the firm. The table shows the main instruments as at November 2026.

sections.heading: What competence models do the markets use?

blocks.text: There are three models: qualification standards (Australia, the EU), exam and registration (the United States, Japan) and firm level competence duties (the UAE free zones). Most markets mix them.

Australia's professional standards require relevant providers to hold an approved degree and, usually, complete a professional year; the January 1, 2026 deadline for existing providers has passed ([financial adviser education and CPD](/regulations/financial-adviser-education-and-cpd-requirements)). Advisers outside that group still follow [RG 146](/regulations/asic-rg-146-training-requirements), and licensees' responsible managers must meet [RG 105](/regulations/asic-rg-105-organisational-competence). Under [MiFID II](/regulations/mifid-ii-knowledge-and-competence-requirements), staff need an appropriate qualification and at least six months of appropriate experience, and may work under supervision for at most four years until they qualify.

In the United States, [FINRA's continuing education rule](/regulations/finra-continuing-education-requirements) builds on qualification exams with an annual Regulatory Element specific to each registration category. In Japan, every officer or employee who solicits covered securities must be registered, and the JSDA grants the qualification to people who pass its exam ([Japan securities sales representatives](/regulations/japan-securities-sales-representative-qualification)). The DFSA and FSRA instead require firms to ensure employees are competent and trained, without a regulator run exam ([DFSA](/regulations/dfsa-training-and-competence-requirements), [ADGM FSRA](/regulations/adgm-fsra-training-and-competence)).

sections.heading: Which markets set minimum CPD or continuing education hours?

blocks.text: Fixed hours appear in Australia, the EU insurance rules, the DFSA and US state rules; MiFID II, RG 146 and Japan's securities regime do not set hours.

items: **Australia:** at least 40 hours a year for relevant providers (36 for approved part timers), at least 70% approved by the licensee, with minimums in four categories.

**EU insurance:** national mechanisms based on at least 15 hours of professional training or development a year under [IDD Article 10(2)](/regulations/insurance-distribution-directive-cpd-requirements).
**DFSA:** at least 15 hours of structured CPD each calendar year for the Senior Executive Officer, Compliance Officer and Money Laundering Reporting Officer.

**United States:** [investment adviser representatives](/regulations/investment-adviser-representative-continuing-education) need 12 credits a year split 6 and 6 in adopting states; [insurance producers](/regulations/insurance-producer-continuing-education-requirements) follow state rules, such as 15 credit hours per licensing period in New York and a 4 hour update plus 20 elective hours every two years in Florida.

**Japan:** life insurance solicitors complete annual continuing education run through insurers and agencies, in principle for all solicitors since 2009 ([Japan insurance solicitors](/regulations/japan-insurance-solicitor-education-requirements)).

sections.heading: What happens when someone falls behind?

blocks.text: In exam and registration markets, falling behind stops the person from working; in qualification markets, the firm carries the breach.

A FINRA registered person who misses the Regulatory Element becomes CE inactive and must stop all registered activity, and a registration inactive for two consecutive years is administratively terminated. A Japanese securities representative who misses renewal training has the qualification suspended, and continued non completion revokes all qualifications. In Australia, providers who had not met the qualifications standard by January 1, 2026 lost relevant provider status. Under MiFID II, breaching Article 25(1) is a listed infringement for the firm. In Portugal, assigning workers without the required knowledge to housing credit intermediation carries fines of up to EUR 250,000 for companies ([Portugal credit intermediaries](/regulations/portugal-credit-intermediaries-training-requirements)).

sections.heading: What should a multinational standardize and what should it localize?

blocks.text: Standardize the competence framework, role mapping, annual needs review and record model; localize qualifications, exams, registration, hours and cycles, because none of these transfer between markets.

blocks.text: The annual needs review is the strongest candidate for a global standard, because MiFID II, FINRA's Firm Element, RG 146 and the DFSA all expect one in some form. A [competency framework](/glossary/competency-framework) that maps each role to local qualification overlays makes cross border moves visible early, and the guide on [building a training matrix for a bank](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix-for-a-bank) shows how to structure the overlay. Onshore UAE banks also face staff competence standards under the [CBUAE Consumer Protection Regulation](/regulations/uae-central-bank-consumer-protection-training).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry builds the competence framework first, mapping roles, knowledge areas and assessment points to each market's qualification and CPD rules before content is written. That makes one framework serve several regimes, with each record traceable to the rule it satisfies. See [financial services](/industries/financial-services).

faqs.q: Can an Australian financial adviser's qualification be used in the EU?
faqs.a: Not automatically. MiFID II requires staff to meet the criteria each Member State publishes, so an adviser moving to the EU must meet the host country's qualification and experience standard. Australian standards likewise apply their own approved degree list.

faqs.q: Does MiFID II set CPD hours?
faqs.a: No. ESMA's Guidelines require firms to review staff development needs at least annually, keep staff current through continuous professional development and train them before new products are offered, but set no hours. The IDD sets at least 15 hours a year for insurance distribution.

faqs.q: How often must Japanese securities sales representatives retrain?
faqs.a: Qualification renewal training is mandatory every five years from the registration date, and within 180 days for new or returning registrants. Missing it suspends the qualification, and continued non completion revokes all qualifications.

faqs.q: Do onshore UAE banks have competence rules?
faqs.a: Yes. The Central Bank of the UAE's Consumer Protection Regulation and Standards require appropriate staff to be qualified and competent and include a dedicated training, competency and ethical conduct section. DIFC and ADGM firms follow DFSA and FSRA rules instead.
